title: Deep and shallow orthographies

sides.name: Deep (English)
points: Spelling matches pronunciation inconsistently, as in COLONEL and PARADIGM.
Many words break the usual pattern, so readers must learn exceptions word by word.
Children learn to decode slowly, reading only about half of pseudowords correctly in Grade 1.

sides.name: Shallow (Finnish, Korean)
points: Each letter corresponds more or less unambiguously to one phoneme.
Patterns are regular, and Korean even gives similar phonemes similar symbols.
Children learn to decode very quickly and read most pseudowords correctly in Grade 1.

why: Orthographic depth explains why decoding is learned so much more slowly in English than in other alphabetic languages.

title: Phonological and surface dyslexia

sides.name: Acquired phonological dyslexia
points: Pseudoword naming is specifically impaired.
Exception word reading is relatively spared.
A dual-route model places the damage in grapheme-phoneme conversion.
The triangle model places it in phonological processing generally.

sides.name: Acquired surface dyslexia
points: Irregular word reading is specifically impaired, with regularization errors like “deef” for DEAF.
Pseudoword reading is relatively spared.
A dual-route model places the damage in the lexical route, its logogens or their connections.
The triangle model places it in semantic processes generally.

why: Together the two form a classic double dissociation, which dual-route models read as two separate processes.

title: Dual-route (DRC) and triangle models of reading

sides.name: Dual Route Cascaded model
points: Pseudowords and regularity effects come from a dedicated grapheme-phoneme conversion rule system.
Frequency effects come from distinct input and output lexicons, separate from the rules.
Semantics is not implemented, and the lexicons are independent of meaning.
The routes are modular, with different processing assumptions and no interaction except at the output.
It is motivated by double dissociations in patients.

sides.name: Triangle (PDP) model
points: Pseudowords and regularity effects come from statistical regularities learned over many words.
Frequency effects come from more exposure to a word giving better learning for that word.
Semantics is directly involved and supports exception words.
The OP and SP pathways share the same probabilistic learning and interact during learning.
It looks for associations, linking phonology to generalization and semantics to exceptions.

why: Both models cover the same basic reading facts, so the contrast is about mechanism, dissociations against associations.

title: Words and Rules and associative accounts of the past tense

sides.name: Words and Rules (Pinker and colleagues)
points: Regulars come from a symbolic rule such as add -ed.
Irregulars are stored in an associative lexicon sensitive to frequency and phonological similarity.
U-shaped learning is imitation, then a rule applied to everything, then stored exceptions with blocking.
Patient dissociations reflect damage to the rule system or to the lexicon.

sides.name: Associative accounts (Rumelhart and McClelland, Joanisse and Seidenberg)
points: Regular patterns are generalizations learned from many verbs, supported by phonology.
Irregulars are learned in the same system and lean more on semantics.
U-shaped learning comes from input that shifts from mostly irregulars to more regulars.
Patient dissociations reflect damage to phonology or to semantics.

why: The two accounts agree that regular and irregular patterns exist but disagree on whether separate rules and stored exceptions are needed to produce them.

title: Two past-tense patient profiles

sides.name: Broca's aphasia
points: Injury to left anterior brain regions, with poor speech production.
Nonwords are worst, and regulars are a little worse than irregulars.
Matched by damaging phonology in the model.
The regular and irregular gap shrinks when items are controlled for phonology.

sides.name: Wernicke's, Alzheimer's and anomic patients
points: Anomic patients have injury to inferior or middle temporal regions.
Irregulars are worst, below regulars and nonwords.
Matched by damaging semantics in the model.
In semantic dementia, irregular impairment correlates strongly with semantic deficit.

why: The opposite profiles look like a rules and words dissociation, but both follow from damage to phonology or to semantics in one system.

title: Frames of reference

sides.name: Intrinsic
points: Uses the object's own orientation.
The ball is at the chair's front.
Not the frame tested in the rotation tasks.

sides.name: Relative
points: Uses the viewer's own position and orientation.
The ball is to the left of the chair from my viewpoint.
Dutch and English speakers in the lab prefer it.

sides.name: Absolute
points: Uses fixed directions that do not change when the viewer turns.
The ball is north of the chair, or uphill in Tzeltal.
Tzeltal speakers prefer it.

why: The rotation tasks pit relative against absolute coding, so a person's choice after turning around reveals which frame they used.

title: Sign language and spoken language

sides.name: Sign language
points: Visual modality, with the hands, face and upper body as articulators.
Phonology built from hand configuration, location and movement.
Shows categorical perception for phonemic hand configuration contrasts.
Left-lateralized, using Broca's and Wernicke's areas plus visual and superior parietal areas.
Uses space to show relationships between words in a sentence.

sides.name: Spoken language
points: Heard rather than seen, and produced with different articulators.
Phonology described with features of speech sounds.
Shows the familiar categorical perception curves for speech sound contrasts.
Left-lateralized, using Broca's and Wernicke's areas, with more auditory and less visual activity than sign.
Does not use signing space to mark relationships between words.

why: The core language network stays the same across the two modalities, while the sensory areas change with the input.

title: Effects of signing experience and of deafness

sides.name: Signing experience (deaf and hearing signers)
points: Shifts the laterality of motion-perception areas from right to left.
Perhaps because motion perception needs to talk to left-lateralized language networks.

sides.name: Deafness (deaf signers only)
points: Enhances attention to the visual periphery.
Perhaps because hearing people rely more on sound for the far periphery.

why: Hearing signers separate the two causes, because they share the laterality shift but not the peripheral enhancement.

title: Exercise and maturational state hypotheses

sides.name: Exercise hypothesis
points: Early in life, humans have a superior capacity for acquiring languages.
If the capacity is not used early, it declines with maturation, but if it is used, later language learning stays intact for life.
Predicts that people who learned a first language early should learn a second language well at any age.

sides.name: Maturational state hypothesis
points: Early in life, humans have a superior capacity for acquiring languages.
This capacity declines with maturation whether or not it was used.
Predicts that later second-language starters do worse even after learning a first language.

why: Johnson and Newport (1989) found that later starters did worse despite having a first language, which fits the maturational state hypothesis.
